[L548] good opportunity to top of the nitrogen.

[L550]     I was lugging the dewar onto the bed of my pickup when

[L552] Unc came running out, waving something in the air.

[L554]     “Mac!” he shouted. “Get over here. Don't make your old

[L556] man run.”

[L558]     This was as excited as I'd seen him in years.

[L560]     I figured the Steelers must've won, but he panted,

[L562] “It's that girl. Says she's been trying to get a hold a you

[L564] all day. You shadowed your phone again, dint'ya? Anyway,

[L566] she wants'ta make an offer but said she had to talk to you

[L568] first.” He handed me the phone he'd been waving wildly, and

[L570] jabbed a finger towards me, saying “You make sure this

[L572] doesn't fall through. This is your recompense young man.”

[L574]     Poula? Trying to get a hold of me? I sat the dewar

[L576] down and took the phone, shaking. I hadn't realized until

[L578] that moment how much of an impression she'd made on me. I'd

[L580] barely talked to a girl since Rayne passed away.

[L582]     “Hi, MacElray?” she said. “So, I was glad to see you

[L584] called about the classes. Your name's on my wait list for

[L586] next semester, but I wanted to tell you...there's an

[L588] opening in a special training class I'm running here for

[L590] employees of one of our subsidiaries, and I figured since

[L592] you already had some experience, you'd fit right in.
[L594] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 14 / 61>

[L595] They're all from different branches and they're all

[L601]     “Um,” I was a little foggy-headed and I wasn't sure

[L603] how to reply.

[L605]     “Sure, I guess. Yeah.” I said.

[L607]     “Great. Show up at the Nutrielle building at eight

[L609] sharp. You know where it is?”

[L611]     “Wait, tomorrow?”

[L613]     “Yeah, sorry. I forgot. That's the only catch. But

[L615] this could be a really good thing for you. It might even be

[L617] a foot in the door here or at BetaSynth, or wherever.”

[L619]     “I wish I could, but I can't make it into the city

[L621] tomorrow. We've got a lot of work lined up on the ranch,” I

said.

[L625]     “Oh, okay.” She sounded disappointed. “Well...think

[L627] about it. If you show up, you're in. If not... Maybe some

[L629] other time, I guess.”

[L631]     There was a long silence, then we both tried to speak

[L633] at once. “Um...I was going to ask you to join me for dinner

[L637]     “Wow,” I said, astonished.

[L639]     “Don't answer now. Just think about it, okay?”
[L641] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 15 / 61>

[L642]     “Yeah,” I said. “Okay.”

[L644]     Another long pause, then I said, “Unc says you wanted

[L646] to make an offer on the ranch?”

[L648]     “Oh, right. I, um...” And just then, the usual

[L650] hesitation which I'd almost started to appreciate in her

[L652] voice turned a corner and that skittish shiftiness came

back.

[L656]     She said, “I'm not a hundred percent certain, but I, I

[L658] think I can offer seven-fifty, with maybe twenty percent

[L660] down. The thing is, I've got some...research and they're

[L662] going to buy it and usually they pay so much and they

[L664] really like my work and I've got a meeting lined up

[L666] and...well, I should know in the next couple days.”

[L668]     “Alright,” I said, again at a loss for words.

[L670]     “We'll talk about it tomorrow,” she said. “Either on

[L672] the phone or, I hope, over dinner.”

metadata.reasoning_title: Comparing Nellibeth Drafts and Planning Revisions

thoughts.summary: Compared Nellibeth drafts, resolved contradictions, and planned revisions

parts:
These are considerably more useful than a pile of backup copies. They give us something the current STORYO model has been missing: **evidence of the story's evolution, including ideas that were abandoned, plot mechanisms that were replaced, and possibilities that never made it into the submitted version.**

My recommendation is that we use them as a *development corpus*, not simply as alternate copies of one manuscript.

And I see several particularly interesting opportunities.

## 1. There are multiple generations of the story

The first thing that stands out is that these aren't all revisions of the same underlying structure. Some are genuinely different story configurations.

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  **A. The earlier Mac & Poula configuration**

  <text color="secondary" size="xs">Mac & Poula.rtf · approximately 6,500 words</text>
  This version opens with Poula's damp clothing, introduces MacElray as someone already working in the tissue-engineering industry, and develops their relationship through his training at Nutrielle. It has a different sequence of encounters and a different starting point for the mystery. <FileCite ref_id="turn12file4"/>

  <divider color="subtle"/>
  **B. The Night Ride / Menagerie configuration**

  <text color="secondary" size="xs">MacElray's Managerie.rtf · titled *Night Ride, With Meat*</text>
  This version has a dramatis personae, with Tosh and Rennie occupying the family roles later associated with Unc and Rayne. It preserves the damp-clothing mystery, the laboratory horror, and the relationship rupture. <FileCite ref_id="turn12file6"/>

  <divider color="subtle"/>
  **C. The Nellibeth manuscript configuration**

  <text color="secondary" size="xs">Submission, Working, Short Edit, and related files</text>
  This is the more familiar structure: the ranch, the accident, Poula's arrival, Mac's training, the relationship, the concealed organism, the Doug misunderstanding, and the eventual Nellibeth-2 revelation. <FileCite ref_id="turn12file8"/> <FileCite ref_id="turn12file24"/>

  <divider color="subtle"/>
  **D. The exploratory fragments**

  <text color="secondary" size="xs">Nellibeth Scraps.odt · Pony Story II.rtf · Poula Builds A Pony.rtf</text>
  These preserve alternate scenes, abandoned explanations, and possible endings. Some are particularly revealing because they contain material that changes the meaning of the finished story. <FileCite ref_id="turn12file13"/> <FileCite ref_id="turn12file14"/> <FileCite ref_id="turn12file16"/>
</box>

I would not yet assume that this is the chronological order. File names, titles, and apparent completeness are insufficient evidence of revision sequence.

## 2. The scraps may be more valuable than the finished drafts

One particularly interesting example is an alternate ending in *Nellibeth Scraps*.

It contains a conversation in which Unc says:

> "Rayne was the passenger."

That is a radically different revelation from the submitted story's closing structure. The scrap also contains an earlier version of the accident premise involving a car crash, a surviving passenger, and liability for the accident. <FileCite ref_id="turn16file4"/>

This is important for STORYO.

We now have evidence of at least two different configurations of the underlying traumatic event:

- The horseback accident: Mac's drunken behavior, Lizzie's death, Rayne's injury and eventual death.
- The earlier car-accident configuration: a different distribution of responsibility, casualties, and family consequences.

These aren't merely alternate sentences. They are different causal worlds.

The engine should be able to preserve both, compare their consequences, and show how changing one fundamental event changes the rest of the story.

There is another particularly interesting fragment: Poula's laboratory project is explicitly described as something she began with a cow in mind, but which Mac inspired her to turn into Nellibeth-2. That gives us a much clearer view of the emotional and symbolic logic behind the final reveal. <FileCite ref_id="turn13file4"/>

## 3. How I propose we use the collection

I would introduce a new layer into STORYO: **the Draft Archaeology Layer**.

Rather than treating the submitted manuscript as the only authoritative representation, we preserve every draft as a source artifact and construct a history of the story's structural changes.

The process would look like this:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <title size="lg">Draft Archaeology</title>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **Original draft files**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">RTF · ODT · TXT · fragments · notes</text>
  </box>
  <box align="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  </box>
  <box background="surface" border radius="md" padding={3}>
    **1. Document inventory**

    File identity, size, format, content hash, completeness, and apparent relationships.
  </box>
  <box align="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  </box>
  <box background="surface" border radius="md" padding={3}>
    **2. Textual comparison**

    Exact passages, additions, deletions, substitutions, moved scenes, and altered dialogue.
  </box>
  <box align="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  </box>
  <box background="surface" border radius="md" padding={3}>
    **3. Structural comparison**

    Changed events, character relationships, causal dependencies, revelations, and endings.
  </box>
  <box align="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  </box>
  <box background="surface" border radius="md" padding={3}>
    **4. Version graph**

    Branches, merges, abandoned configurations, unresolved alternatives, and transformations.
  </box>
  <box align="center">
    <icon name="arrow-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  </box>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} align="center">
    **STORYO's expanded story model**

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">One story, multiple historical configurations</text>
  </box>
</box>

The critical distinction: textual differences and structural differences must be tracked separately.

A sentence can change without changing the story. Conversely, a single changed sentence can reverse a character's culpability, invalidate a revelation, or alter the entire causal structure.

## 4. Three experiments I particularly want to try

**First: reconstruct the transformation of the central mystery.**

The damp clothes, humidifiers, bathroom boy, hidden laboratory, and Doug's physical transformation are a fascinating cluster. We can trace how these elements were introduced, repositioned, and repurposed.

**Second: compare the endings as competing structural solutions.**

The scraps contain alternate resolutions, including the passenger revelation. The submitted ending instead combines Doug's self-modification, Poula's synthetic horse, the ranch sale, and Mac's employment prospects. We should compare what each ending resolves, what it leaves unresolved, and what it does to the emotional meaning of the story.

**Third: investigate the story's changing family and accident architecture.**

The shift from Tosh/Rennie to Unc/Rayne, and from the earlier car-accident material to the horseback accident, deserves its own analysis. It may reveal which structural elements were fundamental to the story and which were replaceable.

## 5. One important change to our development plan

I would postpone expanding the v0.4 ontology into a larger manuscript model until we've done this comparison.

Otherwise, we risk building a very elaborate representation of one particular draft while overlooking the more interesting fact that the story itself has already undergone substantial structural mutation.

The draft corpus gives us a chance to test the engine against *real mutations performed by the author*, rather than mutations we invent for testing.

That is a much stronger experiment.

**My proposed next deliverable is a Draft Archaeology Report and machine-readable version manifest.** It would identify the documents, distinguish duplicate copies from genuine variants, establish provisional lineage, compare the major plot configurations, and preserve every unresolved question rather than forcing an artificial chronology.

I would treat the submitted manuscript as the current reference configuration, but not as the unquestionable winner of every historical contest. The older drafts may contain material worth recovering, and I don't want us to accidentally throw away the interesting bits while building the machine that is supposed to help us discover them.

They give us something the current STORYO model has been missing: **evidence of the story's evolution, including ideas that were abandoned, plot mechanisms that were replaced, and possibilities that never made it into the submitted version.**

My recommendation is that we use them as a *development corpus*, not simply as alternate copies of one manuscript.

And I see several particularly interesting opportunities.

## 1\. There are multiple generations of the story

The first thing that stands out is that these aren't all revisions of the same underlying structure. Some are genuinely different story configurations.

**A. The earlier Mac & Poula configuration**

Mac & Poula.rtf · approximately 6,500 words

This version opens with Poula's damp clothing, introduces MacElray as someone already working in the tissue-engineering industry, and develops their relationship through his training at Nutrielle. It has a different sequence of encounters and a different starting point for the mystery. fileciteturn12file4

---

**B. The Night Ride / Menagerie configuration**

MacElray's Managerie.rtf · titled *Night Ride, With Meat*

This version has a dramatis personae, with Tosh and Rennie occupying the family roles later associated with Unc and Rayne. It preserves the damp-clothing mystery, the laboratory horror, and the relationship rupture. fileciteturn12file6

---

**C. The Nellibeth manuscript configuration**

Submission, Working, Short Edit, and related files

This is the more familiar structure: the ranch, the accident, Poula's arrival, Mac's training, the relationship, the concealed organism, the Doug misunderstanding, and the eventual Nellibeth-2 revelation. fileciteturn12file8 fileciteturn12file24

---

**D. The exploratory fragments**

Nellibeth Scraps.odt · Pony Story II.rtf · Poula Builds A Pony.rtf

These preserve alternate scenes, abandoned explanations, and possible endings. Some are particularly revealing because they contain material that changes the meaning of the finished story. fileciteturn12file13 fileciteturn12file14 fileciteturn12file16

I would not yet assume that this is the chronological order. File names, titles, and apparent completeness are insufficient evidence of revision sequence.

## 2\. The scraps may be more valuable than the finished drafts

One particularly interesting example is an alternate ending in *Nellibeth Scraps*\.

It contains a conversation in which Unc says\:

> "Rayne was the passenger."

That is a radically different revelation from the submitted story's closing structure. The scrap also contains an earlier version of the accident premise involving a car crash, a surviving passenger, and liability for the accident. fileciteturn16file4

This is important for STORYO.

We now have evidence of at least two different configurations of the underlying traumatic event\:

- The horseback accident: Mac's drunken behavior, Lizzie's death, Rayne's injury and eventual death.
- The earlier car-accident configuration: a different distribution of responsibility, casualties, and family consequences.

These aren't merely alternate sentences. They are different causal worlds.

The engine should be able to preserve both, compare their consequences, and show how changing one fundamental event changes the rest of the story.

There is another particularly interesting fragment: Poula's laboratory project is explicitly described as something she began with a cow in mind, but which Mac inspired her to turn into Nellibeth-2. That gives us a much clearer view of the emotional and symbolic logic behind the final reveal. fileciteturn13file4

## 3\. How I propose we use the collection

I would introduce a new layer into STORYO: **the Draft Archaeology Layer**\.

Rather than treating the submitted manuscript as the only authoritative representation, we preserve every draft as a source artifact and construct a history of the story's structural changes.

The process would look like this\:

## Draft Archaeology

**Original draft files**

RTF · ODT · TXT · fragments · notes

**1\. Document inventory**

File identity, size, format, content hash, completeness, and apparent relationships.

**2\. Textual comparison**

Exact passages, additions, deletions, substitutions, moved scenes, and altered dialogue.

**3\. Structural comparison**

Changed events, character relationships, causal dependencies, revelations, and endings.

**4\. Version graph**

Branches, merges, abandoned configurations, unresolved alternatives, and transformations.

**STORYO's expanded story model**

One story, multiple historical configurations

The critical distinction: textual differences and structural differences must be tracked separately.

A sentence can change without changing the story. Conversely, a single changed sentence can reverse a character's culpability, invalidate a revelation, or alter the entire causal structure.

## 4\. Three experiments I particularly want to try

**First: reconstruct the transformation of the central mystery.**

The damp clothes, humidifiers, bathroom boy, hidden laboratory, and Doug's physical transformation are a fascinating cluster. We can trace how these elements were introduced, repositioned, and repurposed.

**Second: compare the endings as competing structural solutions.**

The scraps contain alternate resolutions, including the passenger revelation. The submitted ending instead combines Doug's self-modification, Poula's synthetic horse, the ranch sale, and Mac's employment prospects. We should compare what each ending resolves, what it leaves unresolved, and what it does to the emotional meaning of the story.

**Third: investigate the story's changing family and accident architecture.**

The shift from Tosh/Rennie to Unc/Rayne, and from the earlier car-accident material to the horseback accident, deserves its own analysis. It may reveal which structural elements were fundamental to the story and which were replaceable.

## 5\. One important change to our development plan

I would postpone expanding the v0.4 ontology into a larger manuscript model until we've done this comparison.

Otherwise, we risk building a very elaborate representation of one particular draft while overlooking the more interesting fact that the story itself has already undergone substantial structural mutation.

The draft corpus gives us a chance to test the engine against *real mutations performed by the author*, rather than mutations we invent for testing.

That is a much stronger experiment.

**My proposed next deliverable is a Draft Archaeology Report and machine-readable version manifest.** It would identify the documents, distinguish duplicate copies from genuine variants, establish provisional lineage, compare the major plot configurations, and preserve every unresolved question rather than forcing an artificial chronology.

I would treat the submitted manuscript as the current reference configuration, but not as the unquestionable winner of every historical contest. The older drafts may contain material worth recovering, and I don't want us to accidentally throw away the interesting bits while building the machine that is supposed to help us discover them.

bash -lc cat > /mnt/data/storyo_archaeology/analyze.py <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import hashlib, subprocess, json, re, difflib, zipfile
root=Path('/mnt/data/storyo_archaeology')
rows=[]; texts={}
for p in sorted(root.iterdir()):
 if p.suffix.lower() not in ['.rtf','.odt','.txt']: continue
 if p.name=='analyze.py': continue
 raw=p.read_bytes(); sha=hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()
 if p.suffix.lower()=='.txt': txt=raw.decode('utf-8-sig',errors='replace')
 else:
  cp=subprocess.run(['pandoc',str(p),'-t','plain','--wrap=none'],capture_output=True,text=True)
  txt=cp.stdout
  if cp.returncode: print('PANDOC ERROR',p,cp.stderr[:200])
 txt=txt.replace('\r\n','\n').replace('\r','\n')
 texts[p.name]=txt
 words=re.findall(r"\b[\w’'-]+\b",txt)
 paras=[x for x in re.split(r'\n\s*\n',txt) if x.strip()]
 rows.append({'filename':p.name,'bytes':len(raw),'sha256':sha,'format':p.suffix.lower(),'words':len(words),'paragraphs':len(paras),'scene_break_markers':len(re.findall(r'(?m)^\s*(?:\*\s*\*\s*\*|\*{3,}|#{3,}|[-_]{3,})\s*$',txt)),'text_chars':len(txt)})
 (root/(p.name+'.extracted.txt')).write_text(txt,encoding='utf-8')
# pairwise normalized similarity ratio
pairs=[]
for i,a in enumerate(rows):
 for b in rows[i+1:]:
  ta=re.sub(r'\s+',' ',texts[a['filename']]).strip().lower(); tb=re.sub(r'\s+',' ',texts[b['filename']]).strip().lower()
  ratio=difflib.SequenceMatcher(None,ta,tb,autojunk=False).ratio()
  if ratio>.15: pairs.append({'a':a['filename'],'b':b['filename'],'similarity':round(ratio,4)})
(root/'inventory.json').write_text(json.dumps({'artifacts':rows,'similarity_pairs':sorted(pairs,key=lambda x:-x['similarity'])},indent=2),encoding='utf-8')
print(json.dumps(rows,indent=2))
print('\nTOP PAIRS')
for p in sorted(pairs,key=lambda x:-x['similarity'])[:30]: print(p)
PY

from pathlib import Path
import hashlib,re,json,difflib
root=Path('/mnt/data/storyo_archaeology')
rows=[]; texts={}
for p in sorted(root.glob('*.extracted.txt')):
 txt=p.read_text(errors='replace'); orig=Path(str(p).replace('.extracted.txt',''))
 if not orig.exists(): continue
 rows.append({'filename':orig.name,'bytes':orig.stat().st_size,'sha256':hashlib.sha256(orig.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),'format':orig.suffix.lower(),'words':len(re.findall(r"\b[\w’'-]+\b",txt)),'paragraphs':len([x for x in re.split(r'\n\s*\n',txt) if x.strip()]),'text_chars':len(txt)})
 texts[orig.name]=re.sub(r'\s+',' ',txt).strip().lower()
pairs=[]
for i,a in enumerate(rows):
 for b in rows[i+1:]:
  ta=texts[a['filename']];tb=texts[b['filename']]
  # token shingles jaccard, robust against inserted sections
  def shingles(s,n=8):
   t=s.split(); return set(tuple(t[i:i+n]) for i in range(max(0,len(t)-n+1)))
  sa=shingles(ta);sb=shingles(tb)
  sim=len(sa&sb)/len(sa|sb) if sa|sb else 0
  if sim>.01:pairs.append({'a':a['filename'],'b':b['filename'],'shingle_jaccard':round(sim,4)})
(root/'inventory.json').write_text(json.dumps({'artifacts':rows,'similarity_pairs':sorted(pairs,key=lambda x:-x['shingle_jaccard'])},indent=2))
print(json.dumps(rows,indent=2)); print('\nTOP PAIRS')
for p in sorted(pairs,key=lambda x:-x['shingle_jaccard'])[:35]:print(p)

report='''# STORYO Draft Archaeology Report 0.1

## Scope and method

This pass inventories the Nellibeth-related material uploaded in the current conversation, extracts readable RTF/ODT/TXT content, computes SHA-256 hashes for raw files that could be materialized, counts extracted words and paragraphs, and compares normalized text. Whitespace is normalized for similarity checks; punctuation and substantive wording are otherwise retained. The reported regex word counts are machine counts, not replacements for an editor’s word-count convention.

The two project reference documents were also read as authored design material: **MODULAR STORY** and **vignette expansion**. They describe a dependency lattice and a non-linear network of modules, with direct narrative links distinguished from resonant thematic/metaphoric links. This is treated as a design constraint for STORYO, not as a generic template to impose mechanically.

## Executive finding

The archive does **not** describe one simple sequence of drafts. It contains at least three distinct narrative configurations, one composite fragment archive, and a cluster of near-identical exports of the current submitted story.

The current *Nellibeth* text cluster is effectively one textual state. *Mac & Poula* and *Night Ride, With Meat* are genuinely different earlier configurations. *Nellibeth Scraps* is a mixed archive containing material from more than one branch and should not be ingested as a continuous draft.

## 1. The apparent current-draft sequence is mostly an export cluster

The following documents normalize to more than 99.98% character similarity in the comparisons made here:

- `NELLIBETH [submission draft].txt` (2025 reference text export)
- `WORKING Nellibeth.odt`
- `SUBMITTED Nellibeth by Nathan McKnight.odt`
- `Nellibeth (SHORT EDIT) by Nathan McKnight.odt`
- `Nellibeth by Nathan McKnight.txt`
- `Nellibeth by Nathan McKnight.rtf`

The differences detected are limited to a trailing `<<<<<>>>>>` marker, the cover-page word-count formatting, and a list/bullet formatting change. No scene deletion, scene movement, changed event, or substantive prose revision was detected in this comparison. In this corpus, “SHORT EDIT” is a filename label, not evidence of a shorter narrative.

The original 2025 submission file has 66,848 bytes according to Files metadata. A second upload with the same filename and byte size could not be read, so duplicate status is probable but not hash-verified. The text export retrieved for the first source is 66,847 bytes; it is a retrieval representation, not the original raw file.

## 2. Distinct story configurations

### A. `Paola's Menagerie` / `BAK MacElray's Managerie.rtf`

Approximately 1,294 extracted words. This is a partial opening/middle and outline, not a complete story. It starts after MacElray and Poula have already met and are spending time together. It contains the damp-clothes motif, the Ethiopian restaurant, the rat in Poula’s coat, the bathroom encounter with the strange boy, and an explicit outline of the remaining middle and ending. The outline says Poula shows Mac the older man who tried to remake himself, and that the company will not renew her contract because of their relationship.

### B. `Night Ride, With Meat` / `MacElray's Managerie.rtf`

Approximately 3,723 extracted words. This is a partial third-person draft with developed scenes and unresolved outline notes. It restores the ranch encounter as an opening, then moves through training, attraction, and the Doug-boy warning. The accident account differs from *Mac & Poula*: Mac tells Poula that Rennie was drunk and that Mac was in the passenger seat. The outline later specifies that Tosh reveals Mac was not the passenger, implying a concealed driver-role reversal.

The companion ODT with the same stem is damaged and could not be extracted. It is not assumed to be a duplicate of the RTF.

### C. `Mac & Poula.rtf`

Approximately 6,200 extracted words, close to the document’s own “About 6500 words” header. This is a coherent early story configuration. MacElray is already working at L-Sys; Poula is a Nutrielle instructor; their relationship develops through training and workplace scenes. The backstory is a car crash involving Rennie, a young couple, and the couple’s teenage daughter. The hidden project is initially misread as another human/“boy”; Doug Lenzler is revealed as the older former executive who made himself younger using Poula’s techniques. Poula’s actual creation is a synthetic pony made for Mac.

The two reconcile, Poula buys the ranch, and the story closes on a toast. Unc’s statement that Rennie was the passenger is the final beat. Importantly, the text immediately before that says Mac was in the driver’s seat and Rennie was drunk. The passenger correction does not by itself establish who was intoxicated. A separate note in `Nellibeth Scraps` explicitly assigns drunkenness to Mac, but that note belongs to a different fragment/configuration and must not be silently imported here.

### D. `Dark Pony Ride` / `Pony Story II.rtf`

Approximately 550 words. This is a short first-person opening fragment set at a Somali restaurant after Mac and Poula have met. It foregrounds Poula’s secret, Mac’s “drunken equestrian accident,” and a dead brother. It ends mid-scene. Its voice, starting point, and accident language make it a useful transition/branch candidate, but the surviving fragment does not establish a reliable parent or date.

### E. `Nellibeth Scraps.odt`

Approximately 3,516 extracted words. This is not a single draft. It interleaves patent dialogue, apartment/lab scenes, Doug and pony material, a Rayne/Lizzie/Nellibeth accident account, bracketed author notes, and incompatible endings. At least two ending paths are visible: one in which the ranch is sold to Lenzler and Poula appears to be with him, and another in which Doug leaves, Poula buys the ranch, Mac and Poula reconcile, and Unc reveals that Rayne/Rennie was the passenger.

It also contains the explicit note `[Lie--Mac was the one who was drunk.]` and a family-relationship note defining Rayne as Unc’s adopted daughter from a second marriage and Mac’s step-cousin. These notes are evidence of authorial exploration, not automatically canonical story facts.

**Recommended treatment:** preserve `Nellibeth Scraps` as a fragment reservoir. Split it into passage-level records, tag each as prose/dialogue/author-note/outline/alternate ending, and assign branch membership only where supported. Leave ambiguous fragments unassigned rather than forcing a lineage.

## 3. What changed between the earlier configurations and current Nellibeth

## Scope and method

This pass inventories the Nellibeth-related material uploaded in the current conversation, extracts readable RTF/ODT/TXT content, computes SHA-256 hashes for raw files that could be materialized, counts extracted words and paragraphs, and compares normalized text. Whitespace is normalized for similarity checks; punctuation and substantive wording are otherwise retained. The reported regex word counts are machine counts, not replacements for an editor’s word-count convention.

The two project reference documents were also read as authored design material: **MODULAR STORY** and **vignette expansion**. They describe a dependency lattice and a non-linear network of modules, with direct narrative links distinguished from resonant thematic/metaphoric links. This is treated as a design constraint for STORYO, not as a generic template to impose mechanically.

## Executive finding

The archive does **not** describe one simple sequence of drafts. It contains at least three distinct narrative configurations, one composite fragment archive, and a cluster of near-identical exports of the current submitted story.

The current *Nellibeth* text cluster is effectively one textual state. *Mac & Poula* and *Night Ride, With Meat* are genuinely different earlier configurations. *Nellibeth Scraps* is a mixed archive containing material from more than one branch and should not be ingested as a continuous draft.

## 1. The apparent current-draft sequence is mostly an export cluster

The following documents normalize to more than 99.98% character similarity in the comparisons made here:

- `NELLIBETH [submission draft].txt` (2025 reference text export)
- `WORKING Nellibeth.odt`
- `SUBMITTED Nellibeth by Nathan McKnight.odt`
- `Nellibeth (SHORT EDIT) by Nathan McKnight.odt`
- `Nellibeth by Nathan McKnight.txt`
- `Nellibeth by Nathan McKnight.rtf`

The differences detected are limited to a trailing `<<<<<>>>>>` marker, the cover-page word-count formatting, and a list/bullet formatting change. No scene deletion, scene movement, changed event, or substantive prose revision was detected in this comparison. In this corpus, “SHORT EDIT” is a filename label, not evidence of a shorter narrative.

The original 2025 submission file has 66,848 bytes according to Files metadata. A second upload with the same filename and byte size could not be read, so duplicate status is probable but not hash-verified. The text export retrieved for the first source is 66,847 bytes; it is a retrieval representation, not the original raw file.

## 2. Distinct story configurations

### A. `Paola'"'"'s Menagerie` / `BAK MacElray'"'"'s Managerie.rtf`

Approximately 1,294 extracted words. This is a partial opening/middle and outline, not a complete story. It starts after MacElray and Poula have already met and are spending time together. It contains the damp-clothes motif, the Ethiopian restaurant, the rat in Poula’s coat, the bathroom encounter with the strange boy, and an explicit outline of the remaining middle and ending. The outline says Poula shows Mac the older man who tried to remake himself, and that the company will not renew her contract because of their relationship.

### B. `Night Ride, With Meat` / `MacElray'"'"'s Managerie.rtf`

Approximately 3,723 extracted words. This is a partial third-person draft with developed scenes and unresolved outline notes. It restores the ranch encounter as an opening, then moves through training, attraction, and the Doug-boy warning. The accident account differs from *Mac & Poula*: Mac tells Poula that Rennie was drunk and that Mac was in the passenger seat. The outline later specifies that Tosh reveals Mac was not the passenger, implying a concealed driver-role reversal.

The companion ODT with the same stem is damaged and could not be extracted. It is not assumed to be a duplicate of the RTF.

### C. `Mac & Poula.rtf`

Approximately 6,200 extracted words, close to the document’s own “About 6500 words” header. This is a coherent early story configuration. MacElray is already working at L-Sys; Poula is a Nutrielle instructor; their relationship develops through training and workplace scenes. The backstory is a car crash involving Rennie, a young couple, and the couple’s teenage daughter. The hidden project is initially misread as another human/“boy”; Doug Lenzler is revealed as the older former executive who made himself younger using Poula’s techniques. Poula’s actual creation is a synthetic pony made for Mac.

The two reconcile, Poula buys the ranch, and the story closes on a toast. Unc’s statement that Rennie was the passenger is the final beat. Importantly, the text immediately before that says Mac was in the driver’s seat and Rennie was drunk. The passenger correction does not by itself establish who was intoxicated. A separate note in `Nellibeth Scraps` explicitly assigns drunkenness to Mac, but that note belongs to a different fragment/configuration and must not be silently imported here.

### D. `Dark Pony Ride` / `Pony Story II.rtf`

Approximately 550 words. This is a short first-person opening fragment set at a Somali restaurant after Mac and Poula have met. It foregrounds Poula’s secret, Mac’s “drunken equestrian accident,” and a dead brother. It ends mid-scene. Its voice, starting point, and accident language make it a useful transition/branch candidate, but the surviving fragment does not establish a reliable parent or date.

### E. `Nellibeth Scraps.odt`

Approximately 3,516 extracted words. This is not a single draft. It interleaves patent dialogue, apartment/lab scenes, Doug and pony material, a Rayne/Lizzie/Nellibeth accident account, bracketed author notes, and incompatible endings. At least two ending paths are visible: one in which the ranch is sold to Lenzler and Poula appears to be with him, and another in which Doug leaves, Poula buys the ranch, Mac and Poula reconcile, and Unc reveals that Rayne/Rennie was the passenger.

It also contains the explicit note `[Lie--Mac was the one who was drunk.]` and a family-relationship note defining Rayne as Unc’s adopted daughter from a second marriage and Mac’s step-cousin. These notes are evidence of authorial exploration, not automatically canonical story facts.

Split it into passage-level records, tag each as prose/dialogue/author-note/outline/alternate ending, and assign branch membership only where supported. Leave ambiguous fragments unassigned rather than forcing a lineage.

## 3. What changed between the earlier configurations and current Nellibeth

The current submitted story preserves a recognizable structural architecture from the earlier material: ranch under pressure, Poula as an invading technical/romantic force, Mac’s attraction and hidden wound, the strange boy/Doug, a concealed biological project, a horse-shaped creation, and a late-stage revelation that changes the meaning of earlier scenes.

But the changes are structural, not merely cosmetic:

1. **Accident system:** the earlier car-crash configuration involves Rennie and strangers (a young couple and their daughter). The current story replaces it with a horseback accident involving Mac, Rayne, Lizzie, and Nellibeth. The consequences become intimate and relational rather than a distant traffic catastrophe.
2. **Culpability:** earlier versions experiment with different seat assignments and different claims about who was drunk. The current story makes the narrator’s lie specifically about Rayne’s drinking, while the narrated event establishes that Mac drank and Rayne abstained. This is a distinct deception structure, not a simple rename of the earlier lie.
3. **Family topology:** the earlier material names Rennie as Tosh’s son and Mac’s cousin; later fragments and the current story use Rayne as a female step-cousin/adopted daughter. Do not merge the kinship facts across branches.
4. **Synthetic creation:** the early pony is a gift for Mac, intended to enable shared riding. The current Nellibeth-2 is tied directly to the dead mare, Rayne, and Mac’s unresolved grief. The organism becomes a memorial/replication object, not just a romantic gesture.
5. **Revelation placement:** in *Mac & Poula*, the passenger correction is the final beat, after reconciliation and the pony reveal. In the current story, Mac’s culpability is exposed earlier by Unc, contributing to the relationship rupture. The story then has another revelation sequence: Doug’s self-modification and the identity of Nellibeth-2.
6. **Ending function:** the current job-interview coda absorbs the personal catastrophe into professional identity and institutional value. The earlier branch ends on an unresolved moral correction; the current branch adds a new normalization layer.

This is a substantial transformation of the story’s causal and ethical architecture.

## 4. The author’s modular model is already visible in the material

The **MODULAR STORY** document defines a five-layer “Bio-Tragic Loop”: foundation, incubation, transformation, collapse, synthesis. It explicitly treats the story as a dependency lattice, not merely a sequence of acts, and describes the invariant as a revelation that both fulfills and negates an earlier promise.

The **vignette expansion** document goes further in network terms: Origin/Catalyst, Echo/Reflection, Expansion/Divergence, Convergence/Collapse, and Residual/Afterimage. It distinguishes direct narrative links from resonant thematic/metaphoric links and proposes placing modules by thematic resonance rather than chronology.

The draft corpus validates the need for both layers:

- The **version graph** is not the same as the **story graph**. Drafts branch, recombine, and preserve incompatible world configurations.
- The **story graph** itself needs both causal links and resonant links. A horse can be a plot object, a memory trigger, a mirror, and a symbol without those relations being collapsed into one edge.
- The **reading/presentation order** is not identical to world chronology or causal dependency.
- The author’s notes and narrator’s claims must be kept distinct from established story-world facts.

## 5. Recommended STORYO changes

Do not replace v0.4’s structural-fidelity model. Add a separate Draft Archaeology layer that feeds it.

### New object types

- `Artifact`: uploaded source file with immutable identity, hash, format, and extraction status.
- `TextState`: normalized narrative content state; multiple files may realize the same state.
- `Passage`: source-bounded text segment with paragraph/scene index and provenance.
- `Fragment`: passage whose parent branch or intended placement is unknown.
- `Variant`: a coherent but incompatible configuration of story-world facts and event relations.
- `AuthorNote`: bracketed note, outline instruction, or editorial comment, distinct from story prose.
- `Assertion`: proposition with speaker/source, branch, status (asserted, contradicted, confirmed, unknown), and relation to world fact.
- `Module`: a reusable narrative unit with function and typed links.

### New relation types

`same_text_state_as`, `shares_passage_with`, `reworks`, `branches_from` (only when evidence supports it), `possible_fragment_of`, `contains_alternative`, `contradicts_within_branch`, `echoes`, `inverts`, `causes`, `fulfills`, `negates`, `resonates_with`, and `presented_before`.

### Required safeguards

- Never infer chronology from filenames alone.
- Never merge incompatible accident, kinship, or culpability facts across branches.
- Keep narrator claims separate from established story-world facts.
- Preserve bracketed author notes as authorial annotations, not dialogue or narration.
- Keep thematic/resonant links separate from causal dependencies.
- A fragment may belong to more than one possible branch, or to none yet.
- A source file can be damaged or empty without erasing its identity from the archive.

The key architecture change is to make **version lineage, story-world structure, and modular resonance three related but distinct graphs**.

## 6. File-integrity notes

- `MacElray'"'"'s Managerie.odt`: damaged ZIP structure. Standard extraction fails; ZIP repair recovered settings/manifest only, not the story body. Its RTF companion is readable.
- `Pony.odt`: valid ODT with one empty paragraph and no images.
- `Poula Builds A Pony.rtf`: not RTF. Binary data contains a path into a macOS Spotlight store; no story text recovered.
- Second `NELLIBETH [submission draft].txt` upload: same byte size as the other 2025 source, but retrieval yielded no readable content. Exact duplicate status remains unverified.

## 7. Suggested next move

The best next step is passage-level segmentation of `Nellibeth Scraps`, `Mac & Poula`, and `Night Ride, With Meat`, followed by a branch-aware structural graph. That will let STORYO learn from the actual evolution of this story without inventing a single draft chronology. The current submitted text cluster can remain the reference rendering while the earlier branches remain live, inspectable alternatives.

content.text:
The companion ODT with the same stem is damaged and could not be extracted. It is not assumed to be a duplicate of the RTF.

### C. `Mac & Poula.rtf`

Approximately 6,200 extracted words, close to the document’s own “About 6500 words” header. This is a coherent early story configuration. MacElray is already working at L-Sys; Poula is a Nutrielle instructor; their relationship develops through training and workplace scenes. The backstory is a car crash involving Rennie, a young couple, and the couple’s teenage daughter. The hidden project is initially misread as another human/“boy”; Doug Lenzler is revealed as the older former executive who made himself younger using Poula’s techniques. Poula’s actual creation is a synthetic pony made for Mac.

The two reconcile, Poula buys the ranch, and the story closes on a toast. Unc’s statement that Rennie was the passenger is the final beat, apparently intended as a revelation about the accident account. There is, however, a logic gap in the surviving text: Mac has just told Poula that he was in the driver’s seat, so Unc’s passenger statement does not contradict Mac’s stated seat position. Nor does it establish who was intoxicated. The intended correction may depend on an omitted or changed detail. A separate note in `Nellibeth Scraps` explicitly assigns drunkenness to Mac, but that note belongs to a different fragment/configuration and must not be silently imported here.

### D. `Dark Pony Ride` / `Pony Story II.rtf`

Approximately 550 words. This is a short first-person opening fragment set at a Somali restaurant after Mac and Poula have met. It foregrounds Poula’s secret, Mac’s “drunken equestrian accident,” and a dead brother. It ends mid-scene. Its voice, starting point, and accident language make it a useful transition/branch candidate, but the surviving fragment does not establish a reliable parent or date.

### E. `Nellibeth Scraps.odt`

Approximately 3,516 extracted words. This is not a single draft. It interleaves patent dialogue, apartment/lab scenes, Doug and pony material, a Rayne/Lizzie/Nellibeth accident account, bracketed author notes, and incompatible endings. At least two ending paths are visible: one in which the ranch is sold to Lenzler and Poula appears to be with him, and another in which Doug leaves, Poula buys the ranch, Mac and Poula reconcile, and Unc reveals that Rayne/Rennie was the passenger.

It also contains the explicit note `[Lie--Mac was the one who was drunk.]` and a family-relationship note defining Rayne as Unc’s adopted daughter from a second marriage and Mac’s step-cousin. These notes are evidence of authorial exploration, not automatically canonical story facts.

**Recommended treatment:** preserve `Nellibeth Scraps` as a fragment reservoir. Split it into passage-level records, tag each as prose/dialogue/author-note/outline/alternate ending, and assign branch membership only where supported. Leave ambiguous fragments unassigned rather than forcing a lineage.

## 3. What changed between the earlier configurations and current Nellibeth

The current submitted story preserves a recognizable structural architecture from the earlier material: ranch under pressure, Poula as an invading technical/romantic force, Mac’s attraction and hidden wound, the strange boy/Doug, a concealed biological project, a horse-shaped creation, and a late-stage revelation that changes the meaning of earlier scenes.

But the changes are structural, not merely cosmetic:

1. **Accident system:** the earlier car-crash configuration involves Rennie and strangers (a young couple and their daughter). The current story replaces it with a horseback accident involving Mac, Rayne, Lizzie, and Nellibeth. The consequences become intimate and relational rather than a distant traffic catastrophe.
2. **Culpability:** earlier versions experiment with different seat assignments and different claims about who was drunk. The current story makes the narrator’s lie specifically about Rayne’s drinking, while the narrated event establishes that Mac drank and Rayne abstained. This is a distinct deception structure, not a simple rename of the earlier lie.
3. **Family topology:** the earlier material names Rennie as Tosh’s son and Mac’s cousin; later fragments and the current story use Rayne as a female step-cousin/adopted daughter. Do not merge the kinship facts across branches.
4. **Synthetic creation:** the early pony is a gift for Mac, intended to enable shared riding. The current Nellibeth-2 is tied directly to the dead mare, Rayne, and Mac’s unresolved grief. The organism becomes a memorial/replication object, not just a romantic gesture.
5. **Revelation placement:** *Mac & Poula* places an apparent accident-account correction at the very end, after reconciliation and the pony reveal, although the surviving dialogue does not make the contradiction fully legible. In the current story, Mac’s culpability is exposed earlier by Unc, contributing to the relationship rupture. The story then has another revelation sequence: Doug’s self-modification and the identity of Nellibeth-2.
6. **Ending function:** the current job-interview coda absorbs the personal catastrophe into professional identity and institutional value. The earlier branch attempts to end on a moral correction whose setup appears incomplete; the current branch adds a new normalization layer.

This is a substantial transformation of the story’s causal and ethical architecture.

parts:
They are interesting, and the extra files make the project more promising than a simple draft-comparison exercise. The inventory already shows a wider set than the first pass: alongside the familiar *Working*, *Short Edit*, and *Submitted* texts, there are multiple *MacElray’s Managerie* files, two pony-focused pieces, *Mac & Poula*, and *Nellibeth Scraps*. There are also two exact-size copies of the submitted TXT, which gives us a useful test of whether the archive contains duplicate exports or genuinely distinct textual states.

I'm going to treat this as a small literary-archaeology project, not just feed everything into STORYO. First I'll establish what the files actually contain and how they relate. Then I'll use the differences to improve the engine's model of branching, recombination, and abandoned story possibilities.The first important result: the three files labeled *Working Nellibeth*, *Submitted Nellibeth*, and *Nellibeth (SHORT EDIT)* are not three meaningfully different story versions. After normalizing formatting and whitespace, their text is virtually identical to the 2025 submission draft. The only substantive-looking differences found so far are a marker at the end of the document and a list-formatting change. The “SHORT EDIT” label therefore does not describe a shorter narrative in this corpus. I would group these as **one textual state with multiple document/export forms**, pending a check of the remaining metadata. 

The more interesting material is elsewhere: *Mac & Poula*, *Night Ride, With Meat*, and *Nellibeth Scraps* preserve genuinely different story configurations. They should be represented as branches, not lined up as successive drafts.The archive has yielded something more useful than a draft chronology: **a record of how the story's underlying machinery changed.** Several earlier configurations preserve ideas that the submitted *Nellibeth* has transformed, rather than merely polished.

## What the drafts reveal

| Configuration | What it contains | Status |
|---|---|---|
| *Paola's Menagerie* | Damp-clothes motif, restaurant, Doug's first appearance, early structural outline | Partial |
| *Night Ride, With Meat* | Ranch opening, workplace romance, Doug, and an alternate car-accident account | Partial with outline |
| *Mac & Poula* | Car crash, Rennie, Doug's self-modification, synthetic pony, reconciliation | Coherent early version |
| *Dark Pony Ride* | First-person opening, Somali restaurant, drunken equestrian accident, dead brother | Fragment |
| *Nellibeth Scraps* | Mixed scenes, author notes, alternate accident accounts, and incompatible endings | Composite archive |
| *Nellibeth* | Rayne, Lizzie, Nellibeth, Mac's culpability, Nellibeth-2, and the interview coda | Current submitted story |

The early material is not interchangeable. *Night Ride, With Meat*, for example, has Mac telling Poula that Rennie was drunk and Mac was in the passenger seat. Its ending outline has Tosh reveal that Mac was not the passenger. *Mac & Poula* has a different seat assignment in the surviving dialogue, and its final reveal does not quite contradict what Mac has just told Poula. That's a real textual logic gap, not something I would silently repair. FileCite ref_id="turn21file2" /> <FileCite ref_id="turn21file6" /> <FileCite ref_id="turn23file1" />

The *Scraps* file is particularly valuable. It preserves multiple configurations in the same document, including the explicit note that Mac was the one who was drunk and the family-history note about Rayne. It also preserves more than one ending. Treating it as a continuous draft would contaminate the story model with incompatible facts. FileCite ref_id="turn23file4" />

## The big structural transformation

Three changes stand out.

**1. The wound becomes more intimate.** The early car accident involves Rennie and strangers. The submitted story replaces that with the horseback accident involving Mac, Rayne, Lizzie, and Nellibeth. Mac's deception becomes more specific: he shifts responsibility for his own drinking onto Rayne.

**2. The pony changes meaning.** In *Mac & Poula*, Poula makes a synthetic pony as a romantic gift for Mac, so they can ride together. In the submitted story, Nellibeth-2 is tied directly to the dead mare and Mac's unresolved connection to Rayne. The creation changes from a gift into a memorial and a deeply uncomfortable form of restoration. FileCite ref_id="turn23file9" /> <FileCite ref_id="turn12file9" />

**3. The ending changes its job.** The earlier branch attempts to end with reconciliation and an accident-account revelation. The submitted story moves Mac's culpability revelation earlier, breaks the relationship, then adds the Doug/Nellibeth-2 revelations and the job-interview coda. The tragedy is eventually absorbed into Mac's professional identity. That's a substantial change in the story's ethical architecture.

## One surprising result: the "draft sequence" mostly isn't one

I compared the 2025 submission text, *Working*, *Submitted*, *Short Edit*, and the newer TXT and RTF exports computationally.

<badge color="success">Verified text cluster</badge>

They are more than 99.98% similar after normalizing whitespace. The differences found are document formatting, word-count metadata, a list/bullet change, and a trailing `<<<<<>>>>>` marker. I found no substantive scene revisions in this group. In this collection, *Short Edit* is not actually a shorter narrative.

## What this means for STORYO

The two modular design documents are important here. *MODULAR STORY* describes the Bio-Tragic Loop as a dependency lattice, while *vignette expansion* explicitly describes a network of modules connected by direct narrative and resonant thematic links. FileCite ref_id="turn17file7" /> <FileCite ref_id="turn17file26" />

The corpus suggests that STORYO needs three distinct, interacting graph layers:

- **Version graph:** which artifacts share passages, represent alternative configurations, or possibly branch from one another.
- **Story graph:** what happens, what causes it, what characters claim happened, and what is actually established.
- **Modular resonance graph:** which scenes and motifs echo, invert, fulfill, or negate one another, independently of chronology.

That separation matters. A narrator's false account is not a world fact. A fragment's location in one file does not establish its chronological position. A horse can be a causal plot object, a memory trigger, a mirror, and a symbol at the same time.

I would add a Draft Archaeology layer to v0.4 rather than replace its structural-fidelity engine. The natural next development is passage-level provenance, branch-aware assertions, and explicit author-note handling.

## The archaeology package

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <row align="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="archive" size="xl" />
    **STORYO Draft Archaeology 0.1**
    <spacer />
    <badge color="success">Created and verified</badge>
  </row>
  The package includes the report, raw files that could be recovered, extracted text, SHA-256 inventory, normalized comparison results, provisional branch graph, and your two modular-story design documents.

  [Download the archaeology package](sandbox:/mnt/data/storyo_archaeology/STORYO_Draft_Archaeology_0.1.zip)
</box>

Three files need attention: `MacElray's Managerie.odt` is damaged, `Pony.odt` is empty, and `Poula Builds A Pony.rtf` is not actually an RTF document. I preserved them and documented their extraction status rather than pretending they contained readable story text.

**My recommendation:** next, segment *Nellibeth Scraps*, *Mac & Poula*, and *Night Ride, With Meat* into individually traceable passages. That's where the real branching history lives. We can then build the next STORYO layer against actual authorial mutations rather than hypothetical ones.

- **Version graph\:** which artifacts share passages, represent alternative configurations, or possibly branch from one another.
- **Story graph\:** what happens, what causes it, what characters claim happened, and what is actually established.
- **Modular resonance graph\:** which scenes and motifs echo, invert, fulfill, or negate one another, independently of chronology.

That separation matters. A narrator's false account is not a world fact. A fragment's location in one file does not establish its chronological position. A horse can be a causal plot object, a memory trigger, a mirror, and a symbol at the same time.

I would add a Draft Archaeology layer to v0.4 rather than replace its structural-fidelity engine. The natural next development is passage-level provenance, branch-aware assertions, and explicit author-note handling.

parts: Now, keep in mind... superseded drafts aren't evidence of the characters' "actual" alternate histories. They may or may not shed light on how I was thinking about their motivations in the development of the story--but there's also just placeholders, lack of knowing the character yet, etc. The final story stands on its own, and whatever internal logic it has, it has. If prior versions give us some ideas about how to implement Storyo, or if we want to build in some alternate trajectories inspired by the older versions, that could be fun and interesting, but prior versions shouldn't necessarily be considered to have causal relationship to the final draft; although they could in part or in whole.

That distinction is fundamental, and it changes how I think STORYO should handle its source corpus.

I was beginning to treat the draft archive as a kind of developmental genealogy of *Nellibeth*. That's potentially useful as a record of your writing process, but it would be a mistake to turn that genealogy into the fictional world's history.

**The submitted story is its own canonical world.** Its characters, events, motivations, relationships, and causal structure must be derived from that text and whatever interpretive work we do on it. Earlier drafts have no automatic authority over any of those things.

I'd establish the following principles.

## 1. Three separate kinds of material

| Material | What it can establish | What it cannot establish automatically |
|---|---|---|
| Canonical manuscript | The story's represented world and internal logic | Unstated authorial intentions |
| Developmental archive | Earlier writing decisions, abandoned ideas, experiments, uncertainties | Facts about the canonical characters |
| Generated alternatives | Possible trajectories, mutations, and counterfactual worlds | What happened in the canonical story |

An earlier draft might reveal an idea you were exploring. It might also contain a placeholder, a temporary solution, or a character who hadn't yet acquired a coherent identity. We shouldn't presume to know which without evidence.

## 2. Provenance without fictional inheritance

I want to make one important architectural distinction:

A relationship between two documents is not necessarily a relationship between their fictional worlds.

For example:

```python
DocumentRelation(
    source="Mac_and_Poula",
    target="Nellibeth_Submitted",
    relation="shares_material",
    confidence="observed"
)
```

This establishes a textual relationship.

It does not establish:

```python
WorldRelation(
    source="Rennie",
    target="Rayne",
    relation="same_character"
)
```

That second relationship would require an explicit interpretive decision, not an inference from shared names, roles, or plot functions.

## 3. Make alternate trajectories an intentional STORYO feature

This is where the old drafts become especially interesting.

We could use them as a **possibility library**. STORYO could extract candidate mutations and structural configurations from abandoned material, then offer them as possible branches of the canonical story.

For example:

- What if Poula's synthetic horse were primarily a romantic gift?
- What if Mac's accident involved a different kind of culpability?
- What if the Doug revelation resolved the relationship rather than destabilizing it?
- What if the story ended at the ranch rather than being reframed by the job interview?

These would be new counterfactual branches, not claims about the characters' hidden pasts.

Each branch would have its own world state, provenance, and mutation history. The canonical branch would remain untouched.

## 4. A revised governing architecture

I'd formalize this as three distinct but interoperable layers:

<box border radius="lg" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <box gap={1}>
    **A. Canonical world**
    <badge color="success">Authoritative source</badge>
    The submitted story, its internal facts, relationships, chronology, and interpretive uncertainties.
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    **B. Developmental archive**
    <badge color="info">Historical source material</badge>
    Earlier documents, fragments, notes, and textual transformations. No automatic transfer of fictional facts.
  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    **C. Possibility space**
    <badge color="discovery">Exploratory</badge>
    Deliberate mutations, counterfactual trajectories, recombinations, and emergent structures.
  </box>
  <text color="secondary" size="xs">Connections between layers require explicit, typed provenance. No implicit inheritance.</text>
</box>

One additional principle deserves to be built directly into the engine:

**Absence of knowledge is not evidence of absence, and an unfinished characterization is not necessarily an inconsistency.**

This will help prevent STORYO from treating every ambiguity as a defect to repair. Sometimes the ambiguity is productive. Sometimes the author simply hasn't decided yet. Sometimes the character hasn't told us.

I would revise the Draft Archaeology work accordingly: its version graph should describe relationships between artifacts, not assert a causal genealogy of fictional events. And I'd make sure the canonical story model is built independently before allowing archive-derived ideas to influence it.

That gives us something more powerful than a draft tracker: a system that can distinguish **what the story is, how the author explored making it, and what else it might become.**

from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from typing import Any
import copy, hashlib, json

def h(x,n=16):
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(x,sort_keys=True,ensure_ascii=False,separators=(",",":")).encode()).hexdigest()[:n]

@dataclass
class Mutation:
    op:str
    target:str
    args:dict

class Story:
    def __init__(self, model):
        self.records={x["id"]:copy.deepcopy(x) for x in model["records"]}
        self.connections={x["id"]:copy.deepcopy(x) for x in model["connections"]}
        self.dependencies={x["id"]:copy.deepcopy(x) for x in model["dependencies"]}
        self.rules={x["id"]:copy.deepcopy(x) for x in model["rules"]}
        self.metadata=copy.deepcopy(model["metadata"])
        self.parent=None
        self.refresh()
    def snapshot(self):
        return {"records":self.records,"connections":self.connections,"dependencies":self.dependencies,
                "rules":self.rules,"metadata":self.metadata}
    def refresh(self):
        self.state_id="state_"+h(self.snapshot(),20)
    def clone(self):
        return copy.deepcopy(self)
    def path(self, record_id, path):
        x=self.records[record_id]
        for p in path.split("."): x=x[p]
        return x
    def mutate(self,m):
        c=self.clone()
        if m.op=="set_record":
            rec=c.records[m.target]
            for k,v in m.args.items():
                parts=k.split(".")
                cur=rec
                for p in parts[:-1]: cur=cur[p]
                cur[parts[-1]]=v
        elif m.op=="set_order":
            c.records[m.target][m.args["axis"]]=m.args["value"]
        elif m.op=="change_connection":
            c.connections[m.target]["type"]=m.args["type"]
        elif m.op=="remove_connection":
            c.connections.pop(m.target,None)
        else: raise ValueError(m.op)
        c.parent=self.state_id
        c.refresh()
        return c
    def inspect(self, candidate, m):
        out=[]
        # Dangling endpoints are structural defects, not an automatic veto.
        for rid,c in candidate.connections.items():
            for end in ("from","to"):
                if c[end] not in candidate.records:
                    out.append({"class":"disconnection","severity":"error","item":rid,
                                "detail":f"{end} endpoint {c[end]} is missing"})
        # Source-supported relation changes are reported, never protected by fiat.
        if m.target in candidate.connections and m.op=="change_connection":
            old=self.connections[m.target]["type"]; new=candidate.connections[m.target]["type"]
            if old!=new:
                out.append({"class":"direct_change","severity":"info","item":m.target,
                            "detail":f"connection changed: {old} -> {new}"})
        # Compare concrete records and assertions. Conflicts are diagnostics.
        for rule in candidate.rules.values():
            ids=rule["records"]
            if rule["kind"]=="record_consistency" and rule["id"]=="K_PROJECT_ID":
                a=candidate.path(ids[0],"data.identity"); b=candidate.path(ids[1],"data.project_identity")
                if a!=b:
                    out.append({"class":"contradiction","severity":"warning","item":rule["id"],
                                "detail":f"project identity differs: appearance={a!r}; later identification={b!r}"})
            if rule["id"]=="K_ACCIDENT_ACCOUNTS":
                vals=[candidate.path(ids[i],rule["paths"][i]) for i in range(3)]
                if vals==[False,True,False]:
                    out.append({"class":"source_supported_difference","severity":"info","item":rule["id"],
                                "detail":"the original discrepancy is intact: Mac's account differs from the depicted accident; Unc's account agrees with it"})
                else:
                    out.append({"class":"difference_pattern_changed","severity":"warning","item":rule["id"],
                                "detail":f"Rayne-drinking values across accident/Mac/Unc records: {vals}"})
            if rule["id"]=="K_PATENT_CAUSE":
                claim=candidate.path(ids[0],"data.nutrielle_claims")
                setback=candidate.path(ids[1],"data.occurs")
                if not claim and setback:
                    out.append({"class":"contradiction","severity":"warning","item":rule["id"],
                                "detail":"patent setback remains, but Nutrielle claim record is now false"})
        # Chronology is measured on separate axes. Ordering changes do not rewrite world order.
        for axis in ("world_order","presentation_order"):
            vals=[(r["id"],r.get(axis)) for r in candidate.records.values() if r.get(axis) is not None]
            ordered=sorted(vals,key=lambda z:z[1])
            if len({v for _,v in ordered})<len(ordered):
                out.append({"class":"temporal_collision","severity":"warning","item":axis,
                            "detail":"two or more records share an order coordinate"})
        # Calculate dependency reachability from the changed record/connection, without assuming failure.
        touched={m.target}
        if m.target in candidate.connections:
            touched|={candidate.connections[m.target]["from"],candidate.connections[m.target]["to"]}
        propagation=[]
        changed=True
        while changed:
            changed=False
            for d in candidate.dependencies.values():
                members=set(d["inputs"]+[d["output"]])
                if touched & members and not members<=touched:
                    newly=members-touched
                    touched|=newly
                    propagation.append({"dependency":d["id"],"reached":sorted(newly)})
                    changed=True
        # Functional loss is a relation/function report, not a verdict.
        for d in candidate.dependencies.values():
            members=set(d["inputs"]+[d["output"]])
            if m.target in members:
                propagation.append({"dependency":d["id"],"note":"mutation touches a recorded multi-input structure; inspect whether its function survives"})
        return {"diagnostics":out,"propagation":propagation,"affected_ids":sorted(touched)}
    def transact(self,m):
        c=self.mutate(m)
        report=self.inspect(c,m)
        # Only malformed endpoint references prevent a commit. Contradictions and functional changes survive.
        fatal=any(x["severity"]=="error" for x in report["diagnostics"])
        return (self if fatal else c), {
            "parent_state":self.state_id,"candidate_state":c.state_id,
            "committed_state":self.state_id if fatal else c.state_id,
            "outcome":"blocked_malformed_structure" if fatal else "committed",
            "mutation":asdict(m),"report":report
        }

## Scope and method

This pass inventories the Nellibeth-related material uploaded in the current conversation, extracts readable RTF/ODT/TXT content, computes SHA-256 hashes for raw files that could be materialized, counts extracted words and paragraphs, and compares normalized text. Whitespace is normalized for similarity checks; punctuation and substantive wording are otherwise retained. The reported regex word counts are machine counts, not replacements for an editor’s word-count convention.

The two project reference documents were also read as authored design material: **MODULAR STORY** and **vignette expansion**. They describe a dependency lattice and a non-linear network of modules, with direct narrative links distinguished from resonant thematic/metaphoric links. This is treated as a design constraint for STORYO, not as a generic template to impose mechanically.

## Executive finding

## 1. The apparent current-draft sequence is mostly an export cluster

- `NELLIBETH [submission draft].txt` (2025 reference text export)

- `SUBMITTED Nellibeth by Nathan McKnight.odt`
- `Nellibeth (SHORT EDIT) by Nathan McKnight.odt`
- `Nellibeth by Nathan McKnight.txt`
- `Nellibeth by Nathan McKnight.rtf`

The differences detected are limited to a trailing `<<<<<>>>>>` marker, the cover-page word-count formatting, and a list/bullet formatting change. No scene deletion, scene movement, changed event, or substantive prose revision was detected in this comparison. ### A. `Paola's Menagerie` / `BAK MacElray's Managerie.rtf`

Approximately 1,294 extracted words. This is a partial opening/middle and outline, not a complete story. It starts after MacElray and Poula have already met and are spending time together. Approximately 3,723 extracted words. This is a partial third-person draft with developed scenes and unresolved outline notes. ### C. `Mac & Poula.rtf`

Approximately 6,200 extracted words, close to the document’s own “About 6500 words” header. This is a coherent early story configuration. This is a distinct deception structure, not a simple rename of the earlier lie.
3. **Family topology:** the earlier material names Rennie as Tosh’s son and Mac’s cousin; later fragments and the current story use Rayne as a female step-cousin/adopted daughter. Do not merge the

ral-fidelity model. Add a separate Draft Archaeology layer that feeds it.

### New object types

- `Artifact`: uploaded source file with immutable identity, hash, format, and extraction status.
- `TextState`: normalized narrative content state; multiple files may realize the same state.
- `Passage`: source-bounded text segment with paragraph/scene index and provenance.
- `Fragment`: passage whose parent branch or intended placement is unknown.
- `Variant`: a coherent but incompatible configuration of story-world facts and event relations.
- `AuthorNote`: bracketed note, outline instruction, or editorial comment, distinct from story prose.
- `Assertion`: proposition with speaker/source, branch, status (asserted, contradicted, confirmed, unknown), and relation to world fact.
- `Module`: a reusable narrative unit with function and typed links.

### New relation types

`same_text_state_as`, `shares_passage_with`, `reworks`, `branches_from` (only when evidence supports it), `possible_fragment_of`, `contains_alternative`, `contradicts_within_branch`, `echoes`, `inverts`, `causes`, `fulfills`, `negates`, `resonates_with`, and `presented_before`.

### Required safeguards

- Never infer chronology from filenames alone.

- Keep thematic/resonant links separate from causal dependencies.
- A fragment may belong to more than one possible branch, or to none yet.
- A source file can be damaged or empty without erasing its identity from the archive.

The key architecture change is to make **version lineage, story-world structure, and modular resonance three related but distinct graphs**.

## 6. File-integrity notes

- Second `NELLIBETH [submission draft].txt` upload: same byte size as the other 2025 source, but retrieval yielded no readable content. Exact duplicate status remains unverified.

## 7. Suggested next move

The best next step is passage-level segmentation of `Nellibeth Scraps`, `Mac & Poula`, and `Night Ride, With Meat`, followed by a branch-aware structural graph. That will let STORYO learn from the actual evolution of this story without inventing a single draft chronology. It explicitly treats the story as a dependency lattice, not merely a sequence of acts, and describes the invariant as a revelation that both fulfills and negates an earlier promise.

The **vignette expansion** document goes further in network terms: Origin/Catalyst, Echo/Reflection, Expansion/Divergence, Convergence/Collapse, and Residual/Afterimage. It distinguishes direct narrative links from resonant thematic/metaphoric links and proposes placing modules by thematic resonance rather than chronology.

The draft corpus validates the need for both layers:

- The **version graph** is not the same as the **story graph**. Drafts branch, recombine, and preserve incompatible world configurations.
- The **story graph** itself needs both causal links and resonant links. A horse can be a plot object, a memory trigger, a mirror, and a symbol without those relations being collapsed into one edge.
- The **reading/presentation order** is not identical to world chronology or causal dependency.
- The author’s notes and narrator’s claims must be kept distinct from established story-world facts.

## 5. Recommended STORYO changes

Do not replace v0.4’s structural-fidelity model. Add a separate Draft Archaeology layer that feeds it.

### New object types

- `Artifact`: uploaded source file with immutable identity, hash, format, and extraction status.
- `TextState`: normalized narrative content state; multiple files may realize the same state.
- `Passage`: source-bounded text segment with paragraph/scene index and provenance.
- `Fragment`: passage whose parent branch or intended placement is unknown.
- `Variant`: a coherent but incompatible configuration of story-world facts and event relations.
- `AuthorNote`: bracketed note, outline instruction, or editorial comment, distinct from story prose.
- `Assertion`: proposition with speaker/source, branch, status (asserted, contradicted, confirmed, unknown), and relation to world fact.
- `Module`: a reusable narrative unit with function and typed links.

### New relation types

`same_text_state_as`, `shares_passage_with`, `reworks`, `branches_from` (only when evidence supports it), `possible_fragment_of`, `contains_alternative`, `contradicts_within_branch`, `echoes`, `inverts`, `causes`, `fulfills`, `negates`, `resonates_with`, and `presented_before`.

### Required safeguards

- Never infer chronology from filenames alone.
- Never merge incompatible accident, kinship, or culpability facts across branches.
- Keep narrator claims separate from established story-world facts.
- Preserve bracketed author notes as authorial annotations, not dialogue or narration.
- Keep thematic/resonant links separate from causal dependencies.
- A fragment may belong to more than one possible branch, or to none yet.
- A source file can be damaged or empty without erasing its identity from the archive.

The key architecture change is to make **version lineage, story-world structure, and modular resonance three related but distinct graphs**.

## 6. File-integrity notes

- `MacElray's Managerie.odt`: damaged ZIP structure. Standard extraction fails; ZIP repair recovered settings/manifest only, not the story body. Its RTF companion is readable.

## 7. Suggested next move

The best next step is passage-level segmentation of `Nellibeth Scraps`, `Mac & Poula`, and `Night Ride, With Meat`, followed by a branch-aware structural graph. That will let STORYO learn from the actual evolution of this story without inventing a single draft chronology.
